chapters.title: General
chapters.text:
> Throughout the SMP, present-tense questions ("Is…", "Does…", "Has…") describe the intended state at the relevant project phase. For projects in planning, read these as "is or will be"; for active or maintenance projects, read them at face value. The phase tag on each question shows when the answer is normally expected to harden into a concrete reference.

Identify the project, the people responsible, and any external regulatory regime that applies. Keep this section short: detail belongs in the thematic chapters that follow.

If you're unsure about the management level (A / B / C) you've selected for the project, see the [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/smp/sciwiz/#management-levels) before proceeding.

questions.title: Title
questions.text:
Provide a clear, descriptive, unique title for the software: the name people use to cite, search and refer to it. Specific enough that someone unfamiliar with the project understands what it is broadly about; short enough to fit on a slide and a CLI prompt.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/identity/#software-title) for more details.

questions.title: Funding
questions.text:
Is the development of the software funded?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/identity/#funding-and-project-context) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Funding sources
follow_up_questions.text: How is the development of the software funded?

item_template_questions.title: Funder
item_template_questions.text: Name of the funder. Use the legal-entity name (e.g., "ZonMw", not "ZM"; "Horizon Europe", not "HE").

item_template_questions.title: Project name
item_template_questions.text: Title under which the funding was awarded (often a working acronym).

questions.title: Authors
questions.text:
List the people who should be credited as authors of the software in citations, registries (Zenodo, Software Heritage) and the CITATION.cff file. A reasonable rule of thumb: someone is an author if they would be listed as an author on the paper that describes this software, were it written today.

For most projects, **Maintainers ⊆ Authors ⊊ Contributors**.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/identity/#authors-vs-maintainers) for more details.

questions.title: Maintainers
questions.text:
List **minimum two** people responsible for the software's development, maintenance, and support.
Why two? Single-maintainer projects regularly become orphans when the author leaves LUMC. A backup maintainer also makes review and merging possible. Please make sure that each maintainer has access to this SMP.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/identity/#authors-vs-maintainers) for more details.

questions.title: Regulated software
questions.text:
Is this software a Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), an in-vitro-diagnostic (IVD) product, or otherwise subject to a sectoral regulatory regime (MDR, IVDR, FDA, etc.)?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/identity/#the-regulated-software-flag) for more details.

answers.label: Yes
answers.advice: **Important!** This SMP is not a substitute for the regulatory artefacts that such software must produce (IEC 62304 software life-cycle records, ISO 14971 risk file, MDR/IVDR technical file, etc.). Please consult the LUMC regulatory-affairs office and treat this SMP only as a high-level overview that complements your regulated documentation.

answers.label: No
answers.advice: "No" here means the software is not regulated as a medical device and is not the subject of a regulated trial workflow.

chapters.title: Motivation
chapters.text: Why does this software exist, and for whom? Funders, reviewers, and your future self all start here. Be concrete: prefer specific examples over abstract claims.

questions.title: Purpose
questions.text:
What are the primary purposes of this software? Select all that apply. Use the most specific category you can.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/motivation-scope/#purpose-categories) for more details.

questions.title: Additional purpose
questions.text: If none of the categories above fit your software's primary purpose, describe it briefly here. Use one short noun phrase; if you find yourself writing a paragraph, the right answer is probably one of the existing categories plus a clarifying note in Problem (next question).

questions.title: Problem
questions.text: Describe the main research or technical problem that this software addresses. Aim for 2–4 sentences that an expert from another sub-field could understand: what is the problem, who suffers from it, why a software solution is appropriate. See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/motivation-scope/#the-problem) for more details.

questions.title: Audience
questions.text: Who is the intended audience or primary user group? Pick the most specific categories that apply. See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/motivation-scope/#audience) for more details.

questions.title: Related / upstream software
questions.text:
List existing software, libraries or pipelines that this project builds on, depends on, or interoperates with.
It makes lineage explicit, which is essential for citation and helps reviewers see what is genuinely new. This is not a full dependency manifest but rather a conceptual lineage. See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/motivation-scope/#related-and-upstream-software) for more details.

item_template_questions.title: Reference URL or DOI
item_template_questions.text: Repository, package-page, or DOI URL. DOI preferred for citations.

item_template_questions.title: Relationship
item_template_questions.text: How does your software relate to it? E.g.: dependency, extends/forks, reimplements, alternative to, interoperates with.

questions.title: Value & need for new software
questions.text:
Describe
* what makes this software valuable compared to existing alternatives, and 
* why developing new software is justified rather than contributing to or reusing an existing tool.

If no real alternative exists, say so - that is itself a strong justification. If you are extending an existing tool, name it in the previous question and explain what was missing.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/motivation-scope/#justify-the-existence-of-a-new-project) for more details.

chapters.title: Risks
chapters.text:
Identify what can go wrong and decide what you'll do about it. This chapter is about risk awareness and proportionate mitigation, not risk prediction; you are not expected to enumerate every future failure mode, just the ones whose probability × impact is high enough that ignoring them would be reckless.

**This SMP does not replace the LUMC Data Management Plan (DMP).** Data-protection details (legal basis, retention, DPIA outcomes) belong in the DMP. The Risks chapter only flags that the software touches such concerns and points to the right document or person.

questions.title: Personal / sensitive data handled
questions.text:
Does this software handle personal or otherwise sensitive data?

- **Yes** if your code reads, stores, transmits or processes such data as part of its normal operation (e.g., a Castor extraction script, a clinical-decision-support API).
- **User-supplied only** if your code is a generic library/CLI/tool that can be used with personal data when the user feeds it that data, but does not handle such data itself (e.g., a statistical analysis library, a plotting tool).
- **No** if neither applies (e.g., a synthetic-data tool, a build-tool plugin).

See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#personal-and-sensitive-data) for more details.

answers.label: Yes
answers.advice: A separate LUMC Data Management Plan is likely required. Confirm a central or your division's data steward. See [LUMC Data Stewardship](https://www.albinusnet.nl/actueel/themas/datastewardship/).

follow_up_questions.title: DMP reference
follow_up_questions.text: Link to or identifier of the corresponding Data Management Plan.

follow_up_questions.title: Data categories
follow_up_questions.text: What categories of personal or sensitive data does the software handle? (E.g., pseudonymized clinical records, identifiable imaging, genetic variants).

follow_up_questions.title: Mitigation
follow_up_questions.text:
What is the contingency plan if something fails? What are the responsibilities, escalation procedures, and commitments in the event of a failure?
Mitigations don't have to be elaborate.

If the mitigation risks are outlined in the DMP, say so explicitly. Check with your departmental SOP, if available.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#risk-mitigation) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Mitigation
follow_up_questions.text:
Briefly describe the design choices that prevent inadvertent data leakage: no telemetry by default, no caching of inputs, log scrubbing, clear instructions for users to anonymize upstream or run in a controlled environment.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#risk-mitigation) for more details.

answers.label: No
answers.advice: "No" means: no personal data, no clinical data, no patient-derived data, no contact data of identifiable people, no data covered by an institutional sensitivity policy. If your software might in the future be applied to such data by a downstream user, that's covered under User-supplied only - pick that instead.

questions.title: Security & access control
questions.text:
Does the software face operational security obligations: authentication, authorization, input sanitization, secret management, vulnerability scanning?

These usually apply to services, APIs, and daemons. Pure libraries, scripts, and notebooks normally do not face these obligations directly. See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#security-access-control) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Security measures
follow_up_questions.text: What security measures protect the software and its data?

choices.label: Role-based access control (RBAC) or permissions system
Network security (e.g., firewalls, VPN, isolated subnets)
Follows institutional or regulatory security policies (e.g., ISO 27001, NEN 7510)

follow_up_questions.title: Additional security measures
follow_up_questions.text: List any additional security measures not covered above.

follow_up_questions.title: Mitigation
follow_up_questions.text:
What is the contingency plan if something fails? What are the responsibilities, escalation procedures, and commitments in the event of a failure?
Mitigations don't have to be elaborate. Check with your departmental SOP, if available.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#risk-mitigation) for more details.

answers.label: No
answers.advice: "No" is correct for libraries and analysis pipelines that don't authenticate users, don't expose network endpoints, and don't process secrets.

questions.title: Compliance & regulatory considerations
questions.text:
Is the software subject to specific legal, institutional, or regulatory requirements? (E.g., GDPR, MDR, Institutional SOP). Check with your departmental SOP, if available.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#compliance-regulatory-considerations) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Additional requirements
follow_up_questions.text: List any additional legal, institutional, or regulatory requirements not covered above.

follow_up_questions.title: Requirements
follow_up_questions.text: To your knowledge, which specific legal, institutional, or regulatory requirements is the software subject to? Tick all regulatory or institutional regimes that apply.

choices.label: GDPR - General Data Protection Regulation (EU data protection)
MDR / IVDR - EU Medical Device Regulation / In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation
Other EU or National Regulations (e.g., Dutch WMO, data processing agreements)
ISO 13485 - Quality Management for Medical Devices
Funding Programme Requirements (e.g., Horizon Europe, NWO, ELIXIR)

questions.title: External dependencies
questions.text:
Does the software face (long-term) risks in external software, data, hardware or services whose behavior, availability, or license?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#external-dependency-risks) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Risk details
follow_up_questions.text:
Identify external software, data, hardware or services whose behavior, availability, or license may pose a long-term risk. Be realistic: focus on dependencies that would be expensive to replace, not every transitive package.

Four archetypes worth flagging: vendor lock-in, unstable upstream API, abandoned upstream, proprietary data formats.

follow_up_questions.title: Mitigation
follow_up_questions.text:
What is the contingency plan if something fails? What are the responsibilities, escalation procedures, and commitments in the event of a failure?
Mitigations don't have to be elaborate. Check with your departmental SOP, if available.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#risk-mitigation) for more details.

chapters.title: Planning
chapters.text: Plan resources for three phases of the software's life: development, maintenance, and retirement. Estimates are fine. The goal is to make resource needs explicit so that shortfalls are visible and not deferred.

questions.title: Infrastructure & hardware
questions.text:
What physical or cloud infrastructure and hardware does the project need? E.g.: local servers, HPC allocations (Shark, SURF Snellius), cloud accounts, GPUs (model + VRAM), specialized lab instruments, storage tiers (Research Drive, Object Storage).

**Does NOT include**: version-control hosting, package registries, documentation hosting.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#infrastructure-hardware) for more details.

item_template_questions.title: Details
item_template_questions.text: Briefly mention funding source, access constraints, etc..

questions.title: External services
questions.text:
What external services, partners, or roles do you need from outside your immediate team? Examples: institutional IT/DCC, paid SaaS, hosted CI minutes, legal/contractual support, external review/audit.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#external-services) for more details.

item_template_questions.title: Service / partner
item_template_questions.text: E.g.: External Slack support contract, DCC consultancy, Snellius CPU allocation.

item_template_questions.title: Provider
item_template_questions.text: Organization or platform responsible for the service.

item_template_questions.title: Quantity
item_template_questions.text: E.g.: *0.5 FTE for 18 months*, *5000 CPU-hours*, *€1,200 / year*. Order-of-magnitude is enough.

questions.title: Expertise
questions.text:
List expertise needed to develop, review, deploy, or maintain the software. Focus on gaps that could affect delivery or sustainability: research software engineering, data stewardship, security, regulatory expertise, DevOps, UX, domain knowledge, statistics, testing, documentation, or community management.

Be specific: "Python packaging", "clinical workflow validation", "GitHub Actions CI" is better than "programming". 
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#expertise) for more details.

item_template_questions.title: Quantity
item_template_questions.text: How much of this skill, over what horizon. E.g.: 0.2 FTE for 6 months, one security review before release, ad-hoc consults.

questions.title: Development effort
questions.text:
Estimate the development effort needed to reach a usable version of the software. Use a unit that fits the project: person-days, person-months, FTE over time, sprint count, student project duration, or grant work-package effort.

**Recommended format**: `<FTE-fraction> for <duration>`, e.g., *0.5 FTE for 18 months* or *1.0 FTE-month one-off*. Order-of-magnitude is enough.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#development-effort) for more details.

questions.title: Updates & maintenance
questions.text:
Does the project receive maintenance and updates? (e.g., bug fixes, security patches, feature enhancements).
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#updates-maintenance) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Maintenance level
follow_up_questions.text: What level of maintenance commitment will the project have after active development winds down? Pick the level you can realistically deliver.

follow_up_questions.title: Effort in maintenance
follow_up_questions.text:
Estimate the effort needed to maintain the software after first use or release. Include expected bug fixes, dependency updates, user support, documentation updates, compatibility testing and release work.

**Recommended format**: `<FTE-fraction> per year`. 0 is acceptable, but only if you have an explicit retirement plan.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#maintenance-effort) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Continuity plan
follow_up_questions.text:
Describe what happens if the main developer, maintainer, funding source, or infrastructure becomes unavailable.

Examples of viable answers: backup maintainer with full rights; community fork on day one; archived repository; hand-over to <new responsible entity> at end of grant.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#continuity-hand-over) for more details.

questions.title: Retirement criteria
questions.text:
Select conditions under which the software should be retired, archived, or declared unsupported. Retirement does not always mean deletion; for research software it usually means no new development, clear archival status, and preserved access to relevant releases.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#retirement-criteria) for more details.

choices.label: Change in legal or regulatory requirements
Lack of user demand or adoption

questions.title: Post-retirement accessibility
questions.text:
Will the retired software remain accessible in a read-only, archived, or otherwise retrievable form? Answer "Yes" only if users will be able to find the relevant code, release, documentation, and metadata after active maintenance ends.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#post-retirement-accessibility) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Archive location
follow_up_questions.text: Repository, archive or registry where the retired software will remain findable. E.g.: GitHub archive, GitLab, Zenodo, Software Heritage, institutional archive.

follow_up_questions.title: Retention period
follow_up_questions.text: How long should it remain accessible? E.g.: 10 years after publication.

answers.label: No
answers.advice: Funders increasingly require open archival; consider whether a metadata-only archive is feasible.

chapters.title: Licensing & accessibility
chapters.text: How do people find, retrieve and legally use your software? This chapter covers repository, registries, identifiers, citation, and the license.

questions.title: Repository
questions.text:
Is the source code in a version-controlled repository?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/sharing-licensing/#repository) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Repository URL
Publicly accessible
follow_up_questions.text: Is the repository publicly accessible?

answers.label: No
answers.advice: Closed source is a valid answer when GDPR/IP/MDR/contractual reasons apply, but write the reason down.

follow_up_questions.title: Closed source reasons
follow_up_questions.text: Why is the source not public? Be specific: GDPR, sensitive IP, MDR, contractual obligations, security through obscurity

questions.title: Registries
questions.text:
Is the software listed in community registries? A *registry* is a metadata catalogue (e.g., bio.tools, Research Software Directory), distinct from a package repository that hosts installable artefacts (PyPI, conda-forge, Docker Hub).
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/sharing-licensing/#registries) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Registries list
follow_up_questions.text:
List relevant software registries where the software is listed.
Multiple registries are encouraged: different communities use different ones.

questions.title: Associated persistent identifiers
questions.text:
Does the software have a persistent identifier (PID): a stable, resolvable URL that survives platform migrations and renames? The most common PID is a **DOI** minted by Zenodo when you archive a tagged release.

Recommended workflow: connect your repo to Zenodo → push a tag → create a Release → Zenodo mints a version-DOI and a concept DOI that always points to the latest version.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/sharing-licensing/#persistent-identifiers) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Persistent identifiers
follow_up_questions.text: Specify the identifier system to be used for citing (and versioning) the software.

item_template_questions.title: Identifier type
item_template_questions.text: E.g.: DOI, Software Heritage ID, bio.tools ID.

item_template_questions.title: Associated software version
item_template_questions.text: If it's a concept PID and not a version-specific PID, write "concept".

questions.title: Associated publications
questions.text:
Are there published method papers or preprints for or associated with this software?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/sharing-licensing/#publications) for more details.

questions.title: Software license
questions.text:
Does this software include a license?

Without a license, code is "all rights reserved" by default, even if it is publicly visible: no one (sometimes even you) can legally reuse, fork, or build on it. "Public on GitHub" is not the same as "open source".
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/sharing-licensing/#software-license) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Software license type
follow_up_questions.text:
Pick the license (use the [SPDX identifier](https://spdx.org/licenses/): `Apache-2.0`, not `Apache 2.0`). 
LUMC default: **"as open as possible, as closed as necessary"**.
Recommended license: [Apache-2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0).

follow_up_questions.title: License compatibility
follow_up_questions.text:
Do you check if your dependencies' licenses are compatible with your project's license?

License compatibility means the licenses of your project and its dependencies don't conflict legally. It matters when you use third-party code, such as libraries or modules, because incompatible licenses can block you from distributing your software, force you to adopt more restrictive terms, or even introduce legal risk.

Tooling: licensecheck / pip-licenses (Python), cargo-deny (Rust), license-checker (Node), FOSSA / Snyk / GitHub Advanced Security (cross-language).

See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/sharing-licensing/#license-compatibility) for more details.

answers.label: Yes - manual check
answers.advice: Manual checks are fragile. Acceptable for small projects with few dependencies.

answers.label: No
answers.advice: Risky once the software is shared or released. At minimum, check direct dependencies before publication.

answers.label: No
answers.advice: If you publish code without a license, you're keeping all rights reserved by default. That means nobody else (sometimes even you) has permission to use, modify, share, or extend your work even if it's publicly visible. Just compiling or running the software can constitute a violation. [Read more](https://choosealicense.com/no-permission/) about the implications of not licensing your software.

chapters.title: Documentation & community
chapters.text: Documentation is the most-cited reason that scientific software stops being usable. This chapter covers user-, deployment- and developer-facing documentation, plus the community artefacts that make collaboration possible (code of conduct, contributing guidelines, governance).

questions.title: User documentation
questions.text:
Does the project have user-facing documentation: installation, configuration, usage instructions, at least one runnable example?

- Minimum: a good README answering what / who / how to install / how to run / how to cite / license / how to get support. 
- Preferably: a documentation site (MkDocs, Sphinx+MyST, Quarto, Docusaurus) hosted on Read the Docs / GitHub Pages / GitLab Pages.

See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/documentation-community/#user-documentation) for more details.

questions.title: Deployment documentation
questions.text:
Does the project document how to install, deploy or run the software, including dependencies and environment setup? For reusable or reproducible software, users should not have to infer the environment from source code.

Dependency manifests (the machine-readable lock files (pyproject.toml, requirements.txt, environment.yml, Dockerfile, renv.lock, Cargo.lock, etc.)) is requested in Interoperability chapter.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/documentation-community/#deployment-dependency-documentation) for more details.

questions.title: Developer documentation
questions.text:
Does the project have developer-facing documentation: code organization, build process, how to add a feature, how to run the test suite? The level of detail should match the project level.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/documentation-community/#developer-documentation) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: API reference URL
follow_up_questions.text: For functions or endpoints.

follow_up_questions.title: Contributing guidelines URL
follow_up_questions.text: Recommended: CONTRIBUTING file in the repository.

follow_up_questions.title: Code of conduct URL
follow_up_questions.text: Recommended: CODE_OF_CONDUCT file in the repository.

follow_up_questions.title: Changelog URL
follow_up_questions.text: Recommended: CHANGELOG file in the repository with release details and patch notes

answers.label: No
answers.advice: Acceptable for small one-person scripts, but a risk for continuity if anyone else may maintain the software.

questions.title: Bug reporting & feature request
questions.text:
Do users or collaborators have a clear route to report bugs, request features, or ask support questions? This can be an issue tracker, helpdesk, email address, form or documented contact route.

Recommendation: GitHub or GitLab issue tracker, with issue templates.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/documentation-community/#bug-reporting-feature-requests) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Bug reporting & feature request systems
follow_up_questions.text: List the concrete systems or contact routes used for bug reports, feature requests, or support. Add direct URLs where possible.

questions.title: Governance
questions.text:
How are decisions made when contributors disagree? Who handles releases, docs, security disclosure? What is the decision-making model (lazy consensus / BDFL / formal voting), conflict-resolution path?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/documentation-community/#governance) for more details.

chapters.title: Interoperability
chapters.text: How does the software talk to the rest of the world: which languages, which data formats, which platforms?

questions.title: Programming languages
questions.text:
List the programming languages used in this project, with versions or version constraints.

- The primary language of the codebase.
- Any glue languages with non-trivial logic: workflow DSLs (Snakemake, Nextflow, WDL, CWL), Make/CMake, Bash scripts.
- For container-heavy projects, name the workflow languages.

See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#programming-languages) for more details.

item_template_questions.title: Role in the project
item_template_questions.text: E.g.: "primary library + CLI", "workflow definitions in workflows/".

questions.title: Input data formats
questions.text:
List data formats the software can read or import. Prefer controlled EDAM format terms (or any open, standard, and documented formats) where available. Include constraints only when they matter for interoperability.

Skip if your software does not consume external data.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#input-and-output-data-formats) for more details.

questions.title: Output data format
questions.text:
List data formats the software writes, exports or emits. Prefer controlled EDAM format terms (or any open, standard, and documented formats) where available. Include constraints only when they matter for interoperability.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#input-and-output-data-formats) for more details.

questions.title: Functions
questions.text:
List the functions and operations the software performs.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#functions-operations) for more details.

item_template_questions.title: Command
item_template_questions.text: Relevant command, command-line fragment, or option for executing this function.

questions.title: Interfaces
questions.text:
What are the interfaces (e.g., CLI, API, web) through which the software can be used?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#apis-and-interfaces) for more details.

questions.title: Cross-platform compatibility
questions.text:
Which operating systems (e.g., Linux, macOS, Windows, HPC) and architectures does the software support?

Distinguish *supported* (CI-tested, advertised, bugs accepted) from *expected to work* (used by maintainers but no CI). Pure-runtime languages (Python/R/Java/JS without native deps) usually work everywhere.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#cross-platform-compatibility) for more details.

questions.title: Resource requirements
questions.text:
Describe typical and worst-case hardware resources required to run the software.

Useful structure:
```
Memory     : ~1 GB typical, up to 16 GB for whole-genome inputs
Storage    : ~200 MB code; ~5 GB for a representative input dataset
Compute    : 1–8 CPU cores typical; scales linearly to 32 in batch mode
GPU        : NVIDIA, ≥ 12 GB VRAM, CUDA ≥ 11.8 (segmentation step only)
Wall clock : ~5 min/subject; ~3 h for a 100-subject cohort on 8 cores
```

See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#resource-requirements) for more details.

questions.title: Containerization / environment specification
questions.text:
Does the project ship a complete environment specification beyond the language-level dependency manifest (see Documentation section)? Three patterns, in increasing rigor:
- Lock-file plus README narrative.
- Container image (Dockerfile, Apptainer recipe): gold standard, executable documentation.
- Whole-environment spec (Nix, Pixi, conda-lock): bit-for-bit reproducibility.

See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#containerisation-and-environment-specification) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Environment details
follow_up_questions.text: Path to environment config; registry where built images are pushed (if any).

follow_up_questions.title: Container details
follow_up_questions.text: Path to Dockerfile / Apptainer recipe, registry where built images are pushed (if any).

chapters.title: Testing & quality assurance
chapters.text: How do you (and a future maintainer) know the software still does what it is supposed to do? This chapter covers tests, CI, code quality, and the tooling that keeps a project reproducible.

questions.title: Testing
questions.text:
Does this project have automated tests?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/testing-quality/#minimum-expectations-by-management-level) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Test types
follow_up_questions.text:
Which types of tests do you include for your software? Match the testing depth to the project level and risk.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/testing-quality/#test-types) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Test frameworks
follow_up_questions.text:
Which testing framework do you use? E.g., pytest (Python), testthat (R), Catch2 / GoogleTest (C++), built-in cargo test (Rust), JUnit 5 (Java), Vitest / Jest (JS/TS), bats-core (Bash).
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/testing-quality/#test-frameworks) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Continuous integration
follow_up_questions.text:
Does the project run tests automatically on every push or pull request?

Common CI platforms: GitHub Actions (default for open-source repos), GitLab CI.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/testing-quality/#continuous-integration) for more details.

answers.label: No
answers.advice: Only defensible for small/exploratory scripts. For published results, at least add smoke tests.

questions.title: Project / dependency management tools
questions.text:
Does the project use management tools for project configuration, dependencies, environments, or builds?

E.g.: uv, Poetry, Hatch, Pixi (Python / cross-language); renv, rix (R); cargo (Rust); pnpm / npm (JS); Maven / Gradle (Java); CMake + Conan / vcpkg (C/C++); Snakemake, Nextflow (workflows).
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/testing-quality/#project-dependency-management-tools) for more details.

questions.title: Code quality standards
questions.text:
Do you follow specific software style guide and use tooling for linting/formatting? 

Common combinations: ruff (Python — replaces black + isort + flake8); lintr + styler (R); built-in rustfmt + clippy (Rust); clang-format + clang-tidy (C/C++); eslint + prettier (JS/TS).

Type-checking is separate but worth adding: mypy / pyright (Python), built-in (TypeScript / compiled languages).
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/testing-quality/#code-quality-standards) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Standards & tools for linting/formatting
follow_up_questions.text: Which code quality practices will be used? Include formatting, linting, static analysis, type checking, code review, or style conventions. How do you enforce them? Prefer tools and configuration files over informal intentions.

follow_up_questions.title: Continuous integration / pre-commit hooks
follow_up_questions.text: Does the project run the tools automatically on every push or pull request or as a pre-commit hook?

answers.label: No
answers.advice: Risky for collaborative or long-lived code.

chapters.title: Versioning & release management
chapters.text: How is the project versioned, released and distributed?

questions.title: Version control system
questions.text:
Does the project use a version control system to track source-code changes?

For almost all research software, Git or another version-control system should be used from the start of active development.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/versioning-releases/#version-control) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: System
follow_up_questions.text: E.g.: Git, Mercurial, SVN.

follow_up_questions.title: Versioning scheme
follow_up_questions.text:
How are version numbers assigned? E.g.: SemVer (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) for software with a stable API, CalVer (YYYY.MM.DD, YY.MM) for time-driven projects.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/versioning-releases/#versioning-scheme) for more details.

answers.label: No
answers.advice: Strongly discouraged. For published software or analysis code, this undermines reproducibility and provenance.

questions.title: Software releases
questions.text:
Does the project tag and publish releases?

Recommendation: tag every release on main, create a GitHub/GitLab Release with a changelog, and connect to Zenodo for automatic DOI minting. Keep a CHANGELOG.md.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/versioning-releases/#releases) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Release frequency
follow_up_questions.text: How often do you release new versions of the software?

answers.label: No
answers.advice: Acceptable for internal scripts, weak for software used by others.

questions.title: Software packaging
questions.text:
Do you package you software for distribution?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/versioning-releases/#software-packaging-and-distribution) for more details.

follow_up_questions.title: Distribution channels
follow_up_questions.text:
How will users install the software?

Common channels: language package manager (PyPI / conda-forge / CRAN / Bioconductor / npm / crates.io); container image (Docker Hub / GitHub Container Registry / Quay / Apptainer Library / Biocontainers); source-only (`git clone && pip install -e .`); self-hosted installer; hosted as a service (the user calls your API).

questions.title: Title
questions.text:
Provide a clear, descriptive, unique title for the software: the name people use to cite, search and refer to it. Specific enough that someone unfamiliar with the project understands what it is broadly about; short enough to fit on a slide and a CLI prompt.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/identity/#software-title) for more details.

questions.title: Funding
questions.text:
Is the development of the software funded?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/identity/#funding-and-project-context) for more details.

questions.title: Funding sources
questions.text: How is the development of the software funded?

questions.title: Funder
questions.text: Name of the funder. Use the legal-entity name (e.g., "ZonMw", not "ZM"; "Horizon Europe", not "HE").

questions.title: Project name
questions.text: Title under which the funding was awarded (often a working acronym).

questions.title: Authors
questions.text:
List the people who should be credited as authors of the software in citations, registries (Zenodo, Software Heritage) and the CITATION.cff file. A reasonable rule of thumb: someone is an author if they would be listed as an author on the paper that describes this software, were it written today.

For most projects, **Maintainers ⊆ Authors ⊊ Contributors**.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/identity/#authors-vs-maintainers) for more details.

questions.title: Maintainers
questions.text:
List **minimum two** people responsible for the software's development, maintenance, and support.
Why two? Single-maintainer projects regularly become orphans when the author leaves LUMC. A backup maintainer also makes review and merging possible. Please make sure that each maintainer has access to this SMP.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/identity/#authors-vs-maintainers) for more details.

questions.title: Regulated software
questions.text:
Is this software a Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), an in-vitro-diagnostic (IVD) product, or otherwise subject to a sectoral regulatory regime (MDR, IVDR, FDA, etc.)?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/identity/#the-regulated-software-flag) for more details.

questions.title: Purpose
questions.text:
What are the primary purposes of this software? Select all that apply. Use the most specific category you can.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/motivation-scope/#purpose-categories) for more details.

questions.title: Additional purpose
questions.text: If none of the categories above fit your software's primary purpose, describe it briefly here. Use one short noun phrase; if you find yourself writing a paragraph, the right answer is probably one of the existing categories plus a clarifying note in Problem (next question).

questions.title: Problem
questions.text: Describe the main research or technical problem that this software addresses. Aim for 2–4 sentences that an expert from another sub-field could understand: what is the problem, who suffers from it, why a software solution is appropriate. See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/motivation-scope/#the-problem) for more details.

questions.title: Audience
questions.text: Who is the intended audience or primary user group? Pick the most specific categories that apply. See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/motivation-scope/#audience) for more details.

questions.title: Related / upstream software
questions.text:
List existing software, libraries or pipelines that this project builds on, depends on, or interoperates with.
It makes lineage explicit, which is essential for citation and helps reviewers see what is genuinely new. This is not a full dependency manifest but rather a conceptual lineage. See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/motivation-scope/#related-and-upstream-software) for more details.

questions.title: Reference URL or DOI
questions.text: Repository, package-page, or DOI URL. DOI preferred for citations.

questions.title: Relationship
questions.text: How does your software relate to it? E.g.: dependency, extends/forks, reimplements, alternative to, interoperates with.

questions.title: Value & need for new software
questions.text:
Describe
* what makes this software valuable compared to existing alternatives, and 
* why developing new software is justified rather than contributing to or reusing an existing tool.

If no real alternative exists, say so - that is itself a strong justification. If you are extending an existing tool, name it in the previous question and explain what was missing.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/motivation-scope/#justify-the-existence-of-a-new-project) for more details.

questions.title: Personal / sensitive data handled
questions.text:
Does this software handle personal or otherwise sensitive data?

- **Yes** if your code reads, stores, transmits or processes such data as part of its normal operation (e.g., a Castor extraction script, a clinical-decision-support API).
- **User-supplied only** if your code is a generic library/CLI/tool that can be used with personal data when the user feeds it that data, but does not handle such data itself (e.g., a statistical analysis library, a plotting tool).
- **No** if neither applies (e.g., a synthetic-data tool, a build-tool plugin).

See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#personal-and-sensitive-data) for more details.

questions.title: DMP reference
questions.text: Link to or identifier of the corresponding Data Management Plan.

questions.title: Data categories
questions.text: What categories of personal or sensitive data does the software handle? (E.g., pseudonymized clinical records, identifiable imaging, genetic variants).

questions.title: Mitigation
questions.text:
What is the contingency plan if something fails? What are the responsibilities, escalation procedures, and commitments in the event of a failure?
Mitigations don't have to be elaborate.

If the mitigation risks are outlined in the DMP, say so explicitly. Check with your departmental SOP, if available.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#risk-mitigation) for more details.

questions.title: Mitigation
questions.text:
Briefly describe the design choices that prevent inadvertent data leakage: no telemetry by default, no caching of inputs, log scrubbing, clear instructions for users to anonymize upstream or run in a controlled environment.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#risk-mitigation) for more details.

questions.title: Security & access control
questions.text:
Does the software face operational security obligations: authentication, authorization, input sanitization, secret management, vulnerability scanning?

These usually apply to services, APIs, and daemons. Pure libraries, scripts, and notebooks normally do not face these obligations directly. See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#security-access-control) for more details.

questions.title: Security measures
questions.text: What security measures protect the software and its data?
choices: Role-based access control (RBAC) or permissions system
Network security (e.g., firewalls, VPN, isolated subnets)
Follows institutional or regulatory security policies (e.g., ISO 27001, NEN 7510)

questions.title: Additional security measures
questions.text: List any additional security measures not covered above.

questions.title: Mitigation
questions.text:
What is the contingency plan if something fails? What are the responsibilities, escalation procedures, and commitments in the event of a failure?
Mitigations don't have to be elaborate. Check with your departmental SOP, if available.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#risk-mitigation) for more details.

questions.title: Compliance & regulatory considerations
questions.text:
Is the software subject to specific legal, institutional, or regulatory requirements? (E.g., GDPR, MDR, Institutional SOP). Check with your departmental SOP, if available.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#compliance-regulatory-considerations) for more details.

questions.title: Additional requirements
questions.text: List any additional legal, institutional, or regulatory requirements not covered above.

questions.title: Requirements
questions.text: To your knowledge, which specific legal, institutional, or regulatory requirements is the software subject to? Tick all regulatory or institutional regimes that apply.
choices: GDPR - General Data Protection Regulation (EU data protection)
MDR / IVDR - EU Medical Device Regulation / In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation
Other EU or National Regulations (e.g., Dutch WMO, data processing agreements)
ISO 13485 - Quality Management for Medical Devices
Funding Programme Requirements (e.g., Horizon Europe, NWO, ELIXIR)

questions.title: External dependencies
questions.text:
Does the software face (long-term) risks in external software, data, hardware or services whose behavior, availability, or license?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#external-dependency-risks) for more details.

questions.title: Risk details
questions.text:
Identify external software, data, hardware or services whose behavior, availability, or license may pose a long-term risk. Be realistic: focus on dependencies that would be expensive to replace, not every transitive package.

Four archetypes worth flagging: vendor lock-in, unstable upstream API, abandoned upstream, proprietary data formats.

questions.title: Mitigation
questions.text:
What is the contingency plan if something fails? What are the responsibilities, escalation procedures, and commitments in the event of a failure?
Mitigations don't have to be elaborate. Check with your departmental SOP, if available.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/risks/#risk-mitigation) for more details.

questions.title: Infrastructure & hardware
questions.text:
What physical or cloud infrastructure and hardware does the project need? E.g.: local servers, HPC allocations (Shark, SURF Snellius), cloud accounts, GPUs (model + VRAM), specialized lab instruments, storage tiers (Research Drive, Object Storage).

**Does NOT include**: version-control hosting, package registries, documentation hosting.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#infrastructure-hardware) for more details.

questions.title: Details
questions.text: Briefly mention funding source, access constraints, etc..

questions.title: External services
questions.text:
What external services, partners, or roles do you need from outside your immediate team? Examples: institutional IT/DCC, paid SaaS, hosted CI minutes, legal/contractual support, external review/audit.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#external-services) for more details.

questions.title: Service / partner
questions.text: E.g.: External Slack support contract, DCC consultancy, Snellius CPU allocation.

questions.title: Provider
questions.text: Organization or platform responsible for the service.

questions.title: Quantity
questions.text: E.g.: *0.5 FTE for 18 months*, *5000 CPU-hours*, *€1,200 / year*. Order-of-magnitude is enough.

questions.title: Expertise
questions.text:
List expertise needed to develop, review, deploy, or maintain the software. Focus on gaps that could affect delivery or sustainability: research software engineering, data stewardship, security, regulatory expertise, DevOps, UX, domain knowledge, statistics, testing, documentation, or community management.

Be specific: "Python packaging", "clinical workflow validation", "GitHub Actions CI" is better than "programming". 
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#expertise) for more details.

questions.title: Quantity
questions.text: How much of this skill, over what horizon. E.g.: 0.2 FTE for 6 months, one security review before release, ad-hoc consults.

questions.title: Development effort
questions.text:
Estimate the development effort needed to reach a usable version of the software. Use a unit that fits the project: person-days, person-months, FTE over time, sprint count, student project duration, or grant work-package effort.

**Recommended format**: `<FTE-fraction> for <duration>`, e.g., *0.5 FTE for 18 months* or *1.0 FTE-month one-off*. Order-of-magnitude is enough.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#development-effort) for more details.

questions.title: Updates & maintenance
questions.text:
Does the project receive maintenance and updates? (e.g., bug fixes, security patches, feature enhancements).
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#updates-maintenance) for more details.

questions.title: Maintenance level
questions.text: What level of maintenance commitment will the project have after active development winds down? Pick the level you can realistically deliver.

questions.title: Effort in maintenance
questions.text:
Estimate the effort needed to maintain the software after first use or release. Include expected bug fixes, dependency updates, user support, documentation updates, compatibility testing and release work.

**Recommended format**: `<FTE-fraction> per year`. 0 is acceptable, but only if you have an explicit retirement plan.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#maintenance-effort) for more details.

questions.title: Continuity plan
questions.text:
Describe what happens if the main developer, maintainer, funding source, or infrastructure becomes unavailable.

Examples of viable answers: backup maintainer with full rights; community fork on day one; archived repository; hand-over to <new responsible entity> at end of grant.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#continuity-hand-over) for more details.

questions.title: Retirement criteria
questions.text:
Select conditions under which the software should be retired, archived, or declared unsupported. Retirement does not always mean deletion; for research software it usually means no new development, clear archival status, and preserved access to relevant releases.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#retirement-criteria) for more details.
choices: Change in legal or regulatory requirements
Lack of user demand or adoption

questions.title: Post-retirement accessibility
questions.text:
Will the retired software remain accessible in a read-only, archived, or otherwise retrievable form? Answer "Yes" only if users will be able to find the relevant code, release, documentation, and metadata after active maintenance ends.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/planning/#post-retirement-accessibility) for more details.

questions.title: Archive location
questions.text: Repository, archive or registry where the retired software will remain findable. E.g.: GitHub archive, GitLab, Zenodo, Software Heritage, institutional archive.

questions.title: Retention period
questions.text: How long should it remain accessible? E.g.: 10 years after publication.

questions.title: Repository
questions.text:
Is the source code in a version-controlled repository?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/sharing-licensing/#repository) for more details.

questions.title: Repository URL
Publicly accessible
questions.text: Is the repository publicly accessible?

questions.title: Closed source reasons
questions.text: Why is the source not public? Be specific: GDPR, sensitive IP, MDR, contractual obligations, security through obscurity

questions.title: Registries
questions.text:
Is the software listed in community registries? A *registry* is a metadata catalogue (e.g., bio.tools, Research Software Directory), distinct from a package repository that hosts installable artefacts (PyPI, conda-forge, Docker Hub).
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/sharing-licensing/#registries) for more details.

questions.title: Registries list
questions.text:
List relevant software registries where the software is listed.
Multiple registries are encouraged: different communities use different ones.

questions.title: Associated persistent identifiers
questions.text:
Does the software have a persistent identifier (PID): a stable, resolvable URL that survives platform migrations and renames? The most common PID is a **DOI** minted by Zenodo when you archive a tagged release.

Recommended workflow: connect your repo to Zenodo → push a tag → create a Release → Zenodo mints a version-DOI and a concept DOI that always points to the latest version.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/sharing-licensing/#persistent-identifiers) for more details.

questions.title: Persistent identifiers
questions.text: Specify the identifier system to be used for citing (and versioning) the software.

questions.title: Identifier type
questions.text: E.g.: DOI, Software Heritage ID, bio.tools ID.

questions.title: Associated software version
questions.text: If it's a concept PID and not a version-specific PID, write "concept".

questions.title: Associated publications
questions.text:
Are there published method papers or preprints for or associated with this software?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/sharing-licensing/#publications) for more details.

questions.title: PMID
questions.text: PubMed Identifier (PMID).

questions.title: PMCID
questions.text: PubMed Central Identifier (PMCID).

questions.title: Software license
questions.text:
Does this software include a license?

Without a license, code is "all rights reserved" by default, even if it is publicly visible: no one (sometimes even you) can legally reuse, fork, or build on it. "Public on GitHub" is not the same as "open source".
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/sharing-licensing/#software-license) for more details.

questions.title: Software license type
questions.text:
Pick the license (use the [SPDX identifier](https://spdx.org/licenses/): `Apache-2.0`, not `Apache 2.0`). 
LUMC default: **"as open as possible, as closed as necessary"**.
Recommended license: [Apache-2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0).

questions.title: License compatibility
questions.text:
Do you check if your dependencies' licenses are compatible with your project's license?

License compatibility means the licenses of your project and its dependencies don't conflict legally. It matters when you use third-party code, such as libraries or modules, because incompatible licenses can block you from distributing your software, force you to adopt more restrictive terms, or even introduce legal risk.

Tooling: licensecheck / pip-licenses (Python), cargo-deny (Rust), license-checker (Node), FOSSA / Snyk / GitHub Advanced Security (cross-language).

See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/sharing-licensing/#license-compatibility) for more details.

questions.title: User documentation
questions.text:
Does the project have user-facing documentation: installation, configuration, usage instructions, at least one runnable example?

- Minimum: a good README answering what / who / how to install / how to run / how to cite / license / how to get support. 
- Preferably: a documentation site (MkDocs, Sphinx+MyST, Quarto, Docusaurus) hosted on Read the Docs / GitHub Pages / GitLab Pages.

See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/documentation-community/#user-documentation) for more details.

questions.title: Deployment documentation
questions.text:
Does the project document how to install, deploy or run the software, including dependencies and environment setup? For reusable or reproducible software, users should not have to infer the environment from source code.

Dependency manifests (the machine-readable lock files (pyproject.toml, requirements.txt, environment.yml, Dockerfile, renv.lock, Cargo.lock, etc.)) is requested in Interoperability chapter.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/documentation-community/#deployment-dependency-documentation) for more details.

questions.title: Developer documentation
questions.text:
Does the project have developer-facing documentation: code organization, build process, how to add a feature, how to run the test suite? The level of detail should match the project level.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/documentation-community/#developer-documentation) for more details.

questions.title: API reference URL
questions.text: For functions or endpoints.

questions.title: Contributing guidelines URL
questions.text: Recommended: CONTRIBUTING file in the repository.

questions.title: Code of conduct URL
questions.text: Recommended: CODE_OF_CONDUCT file in the repository.

questions.title: Changelog URL
questions.text: Recommended: CHANGELOG file in the repository with release details and patch notes

questions.title: Bug reporting & feature request
questions.text:
Do users or collaborators have a clear route to report bugs, request features, or ask support questions? This can be an issue tracker, helpdesk, email address, form or documented contact route.

Recommendation: GitHub or GitLab issue tracker, with issue templates.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/documentation-community/#bug-reporting-feature-requests) for more details.

questions.title: Bug reporting & feature request systems
questions.text: List the concrete systems or contact routes used for bug reports, feature requests, or support. Add direct URLs where possible.

questions.title: System
questions.text: E.g.: GitHub issue tracker

questions.title: Governance
questions.text:
How are decisions made when contributors disagree? Who handles releases, docs, security disclosure? What is the decision-making model (lazy consensus / BDFL / formal voting), conflict-resolution path?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/documentation-community/#governance) for more details.

questions.title: Programming languages
questions.text:
List the programming languages used in this project, with versions or version constraints.

- The primary language of the codebase.
- Any glue languages with non-trivial logic: workflow DSLs (Snakemake, Nextflow, WDL, CWL), Make/CMake, Bash scripts.
- For container-heavy projects, name the workflow languages.

See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#programming-languages) for more details.

questions.title: Role in the project
questions.text: E.g.: "primary library + CLI", "workflow definitions in workflows/".

questions.title: Input data formats
questions.text:
List data formats the software can read or import. Prefer controlled EDAM format terms (or any open, standard, and documented formats) where available. Include constraints only when they matter for interoperability.

Skip if your software does not consume external data.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#input-and-output-data-formats) for more details.

questions.title: Output data format
questions.text:
List data formats the software writes, exports or emits. Prefer controlled EDAM format terms (or any open, standard, and documented formats) where available. Include constraints only when they matter for interoperability.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#input-and-output-data-formats) for more details.

questions.title: Functions
questions.text:
List the functions and operations the software performs.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#functions-operations) for more details.

questions.title: Operation
questions.text: Preferably an EDAM Operation term.

questions.title: Command
questions.text: Relevant command, command-line fragment, or option for executing this function.

questions.title: Note
questions.text: Concise comment about this function.

questions.title: Interfaces
questions.text:
What are the interfaces (e.g., CLI, API, web) through which the software can be used?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#apis-and-interfaces) for more details.

questions.title: Cross-platform compatibility
questions.text:
Which operating systems (e.g., Linux, macOS, Windows, HPC) and architectures does the software support?

Distinguish *supported* (CI-tested, advertised, bugs accepted) from *expected to work* (used by maintainers but no CI). Pure-runtime languages (Python/R/Java/JS without native deps) usually work everywhere.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#cross-platform-compatibility) for more details.

questions.title: Resource requirements
questions.text:
Describe typical and worst-case hardware resources required to run the software.

Useful structure:
```
Memory     : ~1 GB typical, up to 16 GB for whole-genome inputs
Storage    : ~200 MB code; ~5 GB for a representative input dataset
Compute    : 1–8 CPU cores typical; scales linearly to 32 in batch mode
GPU        : NVIDIA, ≥ 12 GB VRAM, CUDA ≥ 11.8 (segmentation step only)
Wall clock : ~5 min/subject; ~3 h for a 100-subject cohort on 8 cores
```

See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#resource-requirements) for more details.

questions.title: Containerization / environment specification
questions.text:
Does the project ship a complete environment specification beyond the language-level dependency manifest (see Documentation section)? Three patterns, in increasing rigor:
- Lock-file plus README narrative.
- Container image (Dockerfile, Apptainer recipe): gold standard, executable documentation.
- Whole-environment spec (Nix, Pixi, conda-lock): bit-for-bit reproducibility.

See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/interoperability/#containerisation-and-environment-specification) for more details.

questions.title: Environment details
questions.text: Path to environment config; registry where built images are pushed (if any).

questions.title: Container details
questions.text: Path to Dockerfile / Apptainer recipe, registry where built images are pushed (if any).

questions.title: Testing
questions.text:
Does this project have automated tests?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/testing-quality/#minimum-expectations-by-management-level) for more details.

questions.title: Test types
questions.text:
Which types of tests do you include for your software? Match the testing depth to the project level and risk.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/testing-quality/#test-types) for more details.

questions.title: Test frameworks
questions.text:
Which testing framework do you use? E.g., pytest (Python), testthat (R), Catch2 / GoogleTest (C++), built-in cargo test (Rust), JUnit 5 (Java), Vitest / Jest (JS/TS), bats-core (Bash).
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/testing-quality/#test-frameworks) for more details.

questions.title: Continuous integration
questions.text:
Does the project run tests automatically on every push or pull request?

Common CI platforms: GitHub Actions (default for open-source repos), GitLab CI.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/testing-quality/#continuous-integration) for more details.

questions.title: Project / dependency management tools
questions.text:
Does the project use management tools for project configuration, dependencies, environments, or builds?

E.g.: uv, Poetry, Hatch, Pixi (Python / cross-language); renv, rix (R); cargo (Rust); pnpm / npm (JS); Maven / Gradle (Java); CMake + Conan / vcpkg (C/C++); Snakemake, Nextflow (workflows).
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/testing-quality/#project-dependency-management-tools) for more details.

questions.title: Code quality standards
questions.text:
Do you follow specific software style guide and use tooling for linting/formatting? 

Common combinations: ruff (Python — replaces black + isort + flake8); lintr + styler (R); built-in rustfmt + clippy (Rust); clang-format + clang-tidy (C/C++); eslint + prettier (JS/TS).

Type-checking is separate but worth adding: mypy / pyright (Python), built-in (TypeScript / compiled languages).
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/testing-quality/#code-quality-standards) for more details.

questions.title: Standards & tools for linting/formatting
questions.text: Which code quality practices will be used? Include formatting, linting, static analysis, type checking, code review, or style conventions. How do you enforce them? Prefer tools and configuration files over informal intentions.

questions.title: Continuous integration / pre-commit hooks
questions.text: Does the project run the tools automatically on every push or pull request or as a pre-commit hook?

questions.title: Version control system
questions.text:
Does the project use a version control system to track source-code changes?

For almost all research software, Git or another version-control system should be used from the start of active development.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/versioning-releases/#version-control) for more details.

questions.title: System
questions.text: E.g.: Git, Mercurial, SVN.

questions.title: Versioning scheme
questions.text:
How are version numbers assigned? E.g.: SemVer (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) for software with a stable API, CalVer (YYYY.MM.DD, YY.MM) for time-driven projects.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/versioning-releases/#versioning-scheme) for more details.

questions.title: Software releases
questions.text:
Does the project tag and publish releases?

Recommendation: tag every release on main, create a GitHub/GitLab Release with a changelog, and connect to Zenodo for automatic DOI minting. Keep a CHANGELOG.md.
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/versioning-releases/#releases) for more details.

questions.title: Release frequency
questions.text: How often do you release new versions of the software?

questions.title: Software packaging
questions.text:
Do you package you software for distribution?
See [guidelines](https://lumc-dcc.github.io/rs-guidelines/best-practices/versioning-releases/#software-packaging-and-distribution) for more details.

questions.title: Distribution channels
questions.text:
How will users install the software?

Common channels: language package manager (PyPI / conda-forge / CRAN / Bioconductor / npm / crates.io); container image (Docker Hub / GitHub Container Registry / Quay / Apptainer Library / Biocontainers); source-only (`git clone && pip install -e .`); self-hosted installer; hosted as a service (the user calls your API).
